newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Interest rate fears hold back bourses.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Interest rate fears hold back bourses.

text.p: Leading European shares opened lower on Tuesday, partly on continuing interest rate worries, despite another record close on Wall Street overnight.

On the currency markets, the dollar was steady in thin morning European business and dealers said underlying bullish sentiment was intact, though the U.S. currency slipped overnight from 45-month highs against the yen after Japanese officials again warned against excessive yen weakness.

In London, Europe's busiest stock exchange, shares started mixed and fell lower as sentiment suffered from a scarcity of corporate news and concerns about a possible near-term British interest rate hike and the possibility of tighter U.S. credit.
"People are expecting (UK) rates to go up sometime this quarter but until the rate picture becomes clear the uncertainty will remain and dog the market," one dealer commented.
The FTSE 100 index was down 19 points at 4,087.5 by 1000GMT

In Frankfurt German shares were down in pre-bourse electronic trade and were also weaker when bourse trade began. Dealers cited a steep decline in Japanese stocks overnight and slightly softer German government bonds.

It was a similar story in Paris, where French shares opened lower on weaker bond prices and caution ahead of key U.S. statistics due out later in the week -- Thursday's producer price index and Friday's non-farm payrolls -- which will give clues to future movements of U.S. interest rates.
In foreign exchange, the yen's partial recovery came after comments from finance minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, who said: "An excessively weak or strong yen is not favourable for the Japanese economy."
"We want exchange rates to stabilise," he added.
Analysts regarded the comments as pre-emptive strikes against a quickly falling yen but they said it was unlikely Tokyo would take action to strengthen the currency.
The comeback by the yen did little to boost Tokyo stocks and the Nikkei average fell a sharp 2.83 percent to its lowest close in more than a year on deepening jitters about Japan's economy.

The dollar also slipped against the mark after Bundesbank president Tietmeyer was quoted as saying he saw no need for German interest rate policy to change for the time being. The dollar was around 1.5613 at 1000 GMT from 1.5665 late in Europe on Monday in what dealers described as light volumes and choppy trade.
The only data of note due on Tuesday were U.S. factory goods orders for November due at 1300 GMT, which are forecast to show around a 0.6 percent decline compared with a 0.9 percent rise in October.
The dollar was quoted around 1.5613 marks and 115.25 yen compared with 1.5665 marks and 115.60 yen in late European trade on Monday.
The FTSE 100 index of key British shares was 19.0 points lower at 4,087.5. The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt was 5.84 points down at 2875.06 In Paris, the CAC-40 index was down 6.79 at 2,299.68.
Gold opened at $358.20 an ounce, up slightly from London's previous close of $357.95.
